Fragrantica speaks 21 languages. None of them is Arabic.

The catalogue is normalised and the software is built. It is not launched.

The problem

The world's deepest perfume culture has no encyclopedia of its own.

Three gaps. Every one of them takes about a minute to verify.

Fragrantica publishes 21 language editions. Not one is Arabic.

Hebrew, Mongolian, Ukrainian and Greek each have their own. 46.6 million monthly visitors and 1.74 million members, and no Arabic front door — in the region that wears more fragrance per head than anywhere on earth.

Oud, attar, bukhoor and mukhallat are not categories anywhere.

A global database files a forty-year-old Hindi oud under "woody". No grade, no origin, no wild-versus-cultivated, no burn method. The part of the market Arab buyers care most about is the part no platform describes.

The ratings a Gulf buyer reads were formed in a different climate.

Longevity voted in Berlin does not survive 45°C in Riyadh. Prices show in dollars against Western sellers rather than in SAR or AED against Noon and Ounass. And nothing, anywhere, marks a fragrance halal or alcohol-free.

The product

An encyclopedia built in Arabic, not translated into it.

Six things the platform does that no global fragrance database does at all.

Three languages, from the schema up

Every fragrance, brand, note and accord carries Arabic, English and French as separate columns, not a translation layer over English. Direction flips at runtime with no reload. French is there because the Maghreb is the largest Arabic-speaking audience nobody serves.

Oud graded the way the market grades it

Grade, origin and wild-versus-cultivated, with Hindi, Cambodian, Thai, Kinam and aged oud as distinct first-class types. Attar, bukhoor and mukhallat are categories with their own fields, not tags bolted onto a Western taxonomy.

Votes that match the climate people live in

Alongside longevity and sillage, the community votes performance by climate — hot-dry, hot-humid, temperate, cold — and by occasion: Ramadan, Eid, wedding, prayer. Distributions are shown, never one averaged number, and nothing appears below five votes.

Regional prices, in the buyer's own currency

Noon, Namshi, Sephora KSA, Ounass and Faces in SAR, AED, EGP and KWD, with a best-value-per-millilitre badge. The click goes out to the retailer: no cart, no stock, no returns, no logistics.

Halal and alcohol-free, as a filter

ESMA, SASO and IFANCA certification shown on the fragrance, and alcohol-free as a filter rather than a word buried in a description. For a large part of this market it is the first question asked, and no platform answers it.

The creators this market actually follows

A directory of Arab reviewers with TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and YouTube reach, rated by the community on accuracy, budget range and authenticity. Snapchat is in there because in Saudi Arabia it decides what sells.

How it works

From open data to a living encyclopedia.

Three stages. Two of them are finished.

  1. 01

    Normalise the world's fragrance data

    Six open datasets — a Parfumo corpus, two Fragrantica exports, an Arabic-perfume set, a Kaggle recommendation set and a Hugging Face set — merged into one schema. 249,814 raw records in, 90,579 duplicates removed, 159,235 unique fragrances out. Done, and on disk.

  2. 02

    Enrich it in three languages with Claude

    A Playwright crawler adds images, note pyramids, accords and community ratings: 18,652 perfumes so far, 13,521 of them carrying oud. Claude Haiku writes the Arabic, English and French description, the oud grade and the occasion tags in one batched call per fragrance; Sonnet handles on-demand work. Built and running.

  3. 03

    Open it to the community and let the votes rank it

    Wilson-scored ranking, a five-vote threshold before any rating is shown, and full vote distributions instead of averages. The corpus is the seed; the votes are the part nobody can copy. This is the stage the raise pays for, and it has not started.

Why this wins

A local edition is not a translation.

Three reasons a global platform cannot simply add Arabic and take this market. The table below is the evidence; these are the thesis.

It is a schema problem, not a wording problem

Adding Arabic to Fragrantica gives you Arabic labels on Western categories. It does not give you oud grades, attar subtypes or bukhoor burn methods — those are schema changes to a 119,000-row database that works fine without them, for an audience that rounds to nothing against 46.6 million visitors.

The votes do not port

A global longevity score is the average of everyone, everywhere. Re-voting a whole catalogue for Gulf heat, Ramadan and prayer is not a feature release — it is starting a community over. Whoever collects those votes first holds data the others cannot copy.

The retail graph is regional

Noon, Namshi, Ounass and Faces are where this market checks out, and no global fragrance platform links to any of them. The affiliate relationship and the price feed have to be built locally, one country at a time.

The field

The competition is a good website people read in a second language.

Almost nobody here is choosing between Arabic fragrance platforms. They are choosing between reading English, watching a TikTok, and asking the man in the shop.

Who they areWhat they do well Where they stop
FragranticaThe de facto archive 119,000 fragrances, 2.3 million reviews, 1.74 million members and 46.6 million monthly visitors across 21 language editions. Two decades of community depth nobody can shortcut, and the reference this whole category is measured against.No Arabic edition, no oud grading, no halal status, no climate votes, and not one link to a MENA retailer. Its ratings describe a European wardrobe, and an Arab buyer has to read them in a second language and mentally correct for both heat and price.
Parfumo and ParfumeiThe modern challengers Cleaner apps, barcode scanners, wear trackers and far better collection tools than the incumbent. Parfumei is influencer-first and moves quickly.The same Western catalogue with an English and German centre of gravity. Arab houses appear as entries in it, never as a category with structure of their own — so the fastest-growing part of the market is the part they describe least well.
TikTok and Snapchat reviewersThe real incumbent Where this market genuinely decides what to buy: Arabic, on camera, trusted, immediate and free. No platform we build competes with the trust a Gulf creator already has.Nothing is searchable, comparable or permanent. You cannot filter a video by halal status, sort it by price per millilitre, or find what a creator said about a fragrance eighteen months ago. We index that layer rather than fight it.
Noon, Namshi and OunassWhere the money changes hands The full regional catalogue at real prices, with Arabic storefronts and working logistics. They are the destination of every referral this business earns from.Product pages, not an encyclopedia. No notes pyramid, no community votes, no comparison across sellers, and every commercial incentive to describe a fragrance rather than to judge it.

Stated fairly: a collector who reads English comfortably and buys designer Western fragrance is well served today and has no reason to switch. The wedge is the buyer for whom oud, halal status, Gulf heat and a SAR price are the four things that matter, and for whom every existing option answers none of them.

Market

A market that buys more fragrance per head than any other.

Sized on fragrance retail rather than on beauty as a whole, because the narrower number is the honest one.

Middle East fragrance retail $4.0B → $5.8B +7.5% CAGR · 2025 to 2030
Saudi Arabia — the largest share $1.9B → $2.7B +4.0% CAGR · 2024 to 2033
Our year-three revenue $0 → $1.1M 0.019% of the 2030 market

The third row is the point. A referral business does not capture the market, it captures a commission on part of it — so the claim on the page is deliberately a rounding error against the market it sits in, and it is built from the click upward rather than from the market downward. The arithmetic is in the projections table below, one line per revenue stream, with the rates stated in the model section. Market figures are third-party and are the only numbers on this page not drawn from our own repositories: the region from Expert Market Research ($3.76B in 2024, $4.04B in 2025, 7.5% CAGR), Saudi Arabia from IMARC. The 2030 value is that same source’s base compounded at that same source’s rate, rather than a second house’s headline number — borrowing one report’s base and another’s endpoint is exactly how a table stops tying.

Already built

What exists today, in files that can be opened.

This is the half of the work that does not demo well and cannot be skipped.

A normalised catalogue of 159,235 fragrances

Six open datasets merged into one schema: a Parfumo corpus, two Fragrantica exports, an Arabic-perfume set, a Kaggle recommendation set and a Hugging Face set. 249,814 raw rows in, 90,579 duplicates removed. On top of it, 18,652 perfumes crawled with images, note pyramids, accords and community ratings — 13,521 of them containing oud, across 296 brands.

The API — 18 controllers, 57 endpoints, 29 domain entities

A standalone .NET service of roughly 8,900 lines covering fragrances, brands, notes, accords, perfumers, votes, wardrobes, private notebooks, dupes, layering pairs, retailer prices, influencers and community awards. Wilson-score ranking, GDPR deletion, and background workers for vote recomputation, price refresh, trending and scraping.

Three front ends against the same API

A React storefront of 19 pages in Arabic, English and French — 322 translated strings per language, with direction switching at runtime and no reload. A Flutter module of five screens and nine widgets that drops into the existing OurInc app shell. And a 13-page operations console for catalogue, content, scheduling and analytics.

The Arabic taxonomy nothing else has

110 fragrance notes seeded in all three languages, 25 accords, ten oud types from Hindi to Kinam, attar, bukhoor and mukhallat as categories with their own fields, halal certification, and currency and retailer mapping for all 22 Arab League countries.

A content engine that has actually published

Perfume records drive generated Arabic captions, 4:5 posts, stories and short video, scheduled and posted to Instagram and Facebook. The log carries real post IDs rather than test runs. It is a small thing, but it is the one part of this that has met an audience.

The mechanism

Why the second year costs less than the first.

The catalogue is a cost. The votes are an asset. The distance between those two sentences is the whole business.

The corpus is paid for once

159,000 fragrances were normalised from open data in weeks rather than years. Every competitor's twenty-year archive was assembled by hand; ours is assembled and then enriched by one batched Claude call per fragrance covering all three languages at once.

The votes cannot be bought at any price

Gulf-climate longevity, Ramadan suitability and community-confirmed halal status exist nowhere because nobody has ever asked. Each is a row a competitor would have to re-collect from its own users, in a language it does not publish in, for a market it does not price for.

Wardrobes are why people come back

Owned, wishlist, previously owned and testing shelves, plus a private notebook only the owner sees. A collection someone has spent a year building is switching cost that a fragrance page can never be.

The demand signal is the second product

Which notes, climates, occasions and price bands Arab buyers respond to is something Ajmal, Lattafa, Rasasi and Arabian Oud have no other way to see. It falls out of the community as a by-product and is sold back to the houses in aggregate.

The model

Four ways it earns, none of them holding stock.

Referral only — no cart, no checkout, no inventory, no returns. The rates below are the ones the projection above is built from, so both can be checked against each other.

Retailer affiliate referral · ~6% of order value

Clicks out to Noon, Namshi, Ounass, Faces, Sephora KSA and Golden Scent. Modelled at a $70 average order with 3–4% of clicks converting, which is what produces $363K in year three. The best-value-per-millilitre badge is what makes the click worth taking in the first place.

Brand data and insights · $1,500–2,500 per brand per month

Arab houses see which notes, climates, occasions and price bands their buyers actually respond to, from votes and wardrobes rather than from a commissioned survey. Aggregate only — no personal data leaves the platform. Twelve brands at $2,500 is the year-three line.

Sponsored creator placement · from $1,000 per campaign

The influencer directory already tracks TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and YouTube reach alongside community accuracy scores. Matching a Gulf creator to a brand campaign is a transaction both sides currently do in direct messages with no pricing and no measurement.

Catalogue licensing · $2,000 per storefront per month

The normalised catalogue, the three-language taxonomy and the oud grading, served as an API to retailers and storefronts that need fragrance structure and have none of their own. The smallest line, and the one with almost no marginal cost.

Roadmap

What the eighteen months buy, in order.

Dated against the money below rather than against a wish. The first item is the gap between what is built and what is live.

  1. P1

    Load the corpus and launch — months 1 to 3

    159,235 records into the production database, the first 60,000 enriched in all three languages, and the platform deployed on ourscent.com, which today serves a parking page. Nothing about this is a research project; it is compute, image pipeline and a deploy.

  2. P2

    Seed the community — months 3 to 9

    Arabic fragrance creators in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf brought in as founding reviewers, and the first climate and occasion votes collected. The five-vote threshold means ratings only start appearing once they are real, which makes the early months look slower than they are.

  3. P3

    Turn the referral on — months 6 to 12

    Affiliate agreements with Noon, Namshi and Ounass, price feeds in SAR, AED and EGP, and the best-value badge live. This is the month revenue starts, and the month the model is either right or wrong. It is the milestone the raise is measured against.

  4. P4

    Sell the signal back — months 12 to 18

    The first brand data subscriptions with Arab houses, once the vote corpus is large enough to be worth reading. The mobile module ships inside the existing OurInc app rather than as a separate download, which removes an install from the funnel.

Honest state

What is true today, including the parts that are not flattering.

Written down before you check, because you will, and finding it yourself costs far more than reading it here.

BUILT

The data and the software are real

The corpus, the API, the three front ends and the Arabic taxonomy all exist and are in version control. It is the majority of the build and it is the reason this is a pre-seed conversation rather than a pitch deck.

NOT LIVE

ourscent.com is a parked domain

The domain is registered and currently serves a parking lander. Nothing is deployed on it. Anyone can confirm that in ten seconds, so it is said first rather than last.

ZERO

No users, no votes, no revenue

There is no community, not one vote has been cast, no affiliate agreement is signed and nothing has been earned. The projection starts from nothing on purpose, and the first honest number will arrive somewhere around month nine.

STUBBED

The database holds placeholders, not the catalogue

The API answers correctly and returns test rows today. Loading the 159,235 normalised records into production and enriching them is the first item on the roadmap, not a solved problem — which is also why there are no product screenshots on this page.

SHIPPED

The content engine has actually posted

Generated Arabic captions and imagery have been published to Instagram and Facebook with real post IDs in the log. Small, and it is the only part of this that has met an audience.

ONE PERSON

The whole thing is carried by one operator

Design, backend, both front ends, the data pipeline and the content engine are one person's work. That is why it exists at this cost, and it is also the ceiling that the third line of the raise is meant to lift.

The ask

$200K pre-seed, on a post-money SAFE.

Eighteen months from a built platform to a live one with revenue and a vote corpus nobody else holds. The milestone is signed affiliate agreements and the first commission, not a user count.

  • $200,000 — raising $150K to $250KA standard post-money SAFE. It buys eighteen months of runway against one milestone: a deployed platform, a defensible Arabic vote corpus and the first referral revenue. Reaching that turns a seed round into a different conversation; not reaching it should be visible by month twelve.
  • Launch and data load — about 35%Hosting, the CDN and image pipeline for 160,000 fragrances, and the Claude enrichment cost of writing three languages, oud grades and occasion tags across the catalogue. The largest single line, and it is mostly compute rather than salary.
  • Community seeding — about 35%Paid partnerships with Arabic fragrance creators in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf to bring the first reviewers, and one content editor working in Arabic. The votes are the asset; this is the line that buys the first ten thousand of them.
  • A second pair of hands — about 30%One engineer, so that the single-operator risk named in the section above stops being the ceiling on how fast any of this can move.
